Atlas/Chemistry/Particles & states/Solids, liquids and gases

Chemistry · Particles & states · ABOUT 20 MINUTES

Why can you squeeze air, but barely squeeze water?

A solid keeps its own shape. A liquid flows but keeps roughly the same volume; a gas spreads through the available space. Tiny moving particles help explain these differences.

START WITH A QUESTION

Imagine two identical sealed syringes, without needles: one contains air, the other water. Which plunger would move further under the same gentle push? Predict why before opening the explanation.

Have a guess together before revealing the idea.

The idea underneath +

Matter is made of particles, such as atoms or molecules. In a solid, neighbouring particles stay in fixed positions relative to each other, vibrating rather than sitting perfectly still. In a liquid, particles remain close but move past one another. In a gas, they are much further apart and move freely between collisions. Squeezing a gas mostly reduces the gaps; liquids and solids have much less space to close up.

Why know this?

This explains why air can be compressed into a bicycle tyre and why liquids can transmit a push in hydraulic equipment. A liquid can flow without being easy to compress: those are different properties.

01

A tyre is not full of nothing

Gas particles collide with the tyre walls, producing pressure. Invisible air still occupies space.

02

Pourable does not always mean liquid

Sand pours because solid grains move past each other. Each grain keeps its shape.

03

One substance, different arrangements

Ice and liquid water contain the same water molecules. Melting changes their arrangement and movement, not their identity.

THINK / DRAW / TRY

Make it a conversation.

On paper, draw three boxes labelled solid, liquid and gas. Put twelve identical dots in each: tightly grouped in fixed positions, close but irregular, then widely spaced. Add arrows for vibration or movement. Now sketch each sample in a narrower container. Which sample changes shape, and which can also fit into much less volume? Keep all twelve dots.

One more twist

Sand pours from a cup. Does that make it a liquid? What would you predict if you examined and gently pressed a single grain?

Help me explain this +

The air plunger moves further because gas particles have large gaps between them. The water is only slightly compressible; avoid claiming it cannot compress at all. For sand, distinguish the whole pile from its individual solid grains. Listen for explanations about spacing and movement, not particles shrinking. The drawing is a model: real particles are not pencil dots, and the gaps are not filled with air. Liquids also have attractions between particles. Do not use the regular solid drawing to claim every solid has a perfect crystal pattern.

A common mix-up

Particles in a solid are not motionless. They vibrate around positions even while the whole object stays still.

Think like a scientist

How would you make the syringe comparison fair? Consider syringe size, starting volume, applied force and trapped air bubbles in the water.
